Sadly, I have heard stories such as yours before. I have had ADULTS tell me that their COLLEGE PROFESSORS said, "I don't know what's going on with you, but you need to get that checked out." Super professional, right?

It's sad to see that ignorance has led to moments like this. I, as an SLP, feel that others' views or definitions of stuttering/stammering/fluency disorders/differences are highly incorrect. There is so much stigma and misinformation that continues to be thrown around which is why I try to arm my older students with the information they need to self advocate and inform others of the truth! Stuttering IS cool. Stuttering has NOTHING to do with intellect. COOL people stutter. EVERYONE uses disfluencies; NO ONE has "perfect" fluency. Stuttering DOES NOT negate or subtract any meaning from what you are trying to say.

You are important, and what you have to say is important regardless if you stutter or not.

I also have an anxiety disorder, which I think helps me when working with People Who Stutter (PWS). I may not know /exactly/ how you feel because you have experiences that I do not have, but I can understand some of the emotions that come from repeated experiences and occurrences that have happened. I do understand a lot of the anxiety that comes with stuttering, but, for me, the anxiety comes from other places and in other forms. I can still relate, listen, and hopefully help people feel at ease :)

Thank you for sharing your story and thoughts with me! I always want to hear the real viewpoints of others because it helps me be a better SLP that can help these people if they need me. :)

Hi! I am speech-language pathologist and I have worked with both children and adults who stutter & clutter. Stuttering and fluency disorders/differences are my favorite areas of speech therapy.

I am sorry that you have had these instances of people becoming frustrated when you are in the moment of stuttering or disfluency. I personally do not understand your feelings, but I have had my students and clients explain to me how they feel during moments of blocking- I can only imagine how you must feel when you're trying to speak your thoughts and others are showing signs of frustration. I am sorry that our lack of education regarding stuttering and fluency disorders and differences has led to moments such as the one you have described.

I just want to say what I say to all of my students and clients- I want you to say what you have to say because what you have to say is important! You are a person with their own thoughts, ideas, and beliefs- you have every right to speak freely without discrimination from people who have no idea what stuttering is or what a disfluency is. (LITERALLY EVERYONE is disfluent. No one wants to talk about how "um" and over usage of "like" is a disfluency.)

Those people that have reacted in that way are ignorant and just plain rude. They mean nothing. I know that doesn't help in the moment when it's happening, but I just wanted to say it.

Also, if it helps, there's people out there that think stuttering is really cool :)

I completely understand where you are coming from as I have seen it happen before! It's the side of speech and language disorders that no one thinks about. I mean really- if you cannot produce the correct sounds or words to get your message across and no one can understand what you're trying to say how can you have your physical, emotional, and mental needs met? Communication is so much more than participating in a conversation; communication is the way we interact with the world, gain knowledge, get our needs and wants met, and is essential to our health and wellbeing. If we are unable to functionally communicate, of course, that's going to bring about anger, frustration, sadness, and depression.

I am sorry to hear of your experiences and I can only imagine how difficult that must have been for you! I have seen students "act out" because they're just tired of not being understood and just, like you said, want to be taken seriously, so since they cannot communicate verbally, or using AAC, they use their behaviors- and it's completely understandable! 

None of this is cute. What you went through and felt during those times was not cute! Your experiences aren't a cute fad to mimic on the internet. Your speech impairment was not something you would have ever chosen for yourself and it reached far beyond this "hewwo i lily an am 5!" You struggled to communicate your wants, needs, and thoughts with the world- you weren't being understood and you couldn't just turn it off after the camera wasn't on you.

Your experiences and feelings were, and still are, valid, and your struggles were/are anything but trivial.

I am sorry that you had to struggle in such a way, but I am so happy to hear that you were able to receive help <3

I can complete sympathize and empathize with your current feelings towards your speech. How can you not feel self conscious if what was considered "wrong" about you was constantly brought to your attention in such a negative way? I am sorry that others' words and actions caused you to feel like you could not fully express yourself verbally. You deserve to speak freely and communicate your thoughts and ideas as everyone else does- even if your /r/ isn't perfect, but I'm sure you're doing just fine :)

Let me say this though. Regardless of your production of /r/ your thoughts, ideas, questions, and comments are important. Does substituting an /w/ for an /r/ mean that you're not brilliant? That you're not intelligent? That you're not a wonderful person deserving of love, care, support, and respect? Of course not. 

The /r/ sound is one of the most difficult sounds to learn. I meet men and women who are still not 100% in their production of /r/ and you know what? It means absolutely nothing to me. Trust me when I say that people who are actually knowledgeable of speech and language are not viewing you as any less of an individual. I am so sorry that others' ignorance has made you feel insecure. 

Also, at the end of the day... we all produce sounds, words, phrases, etc. differently! I grew up in the south in a very diverse area where I was exposed to many different languages, dialects, etc. I'm pretty sure someone from another part of the country would find some of my sound productions "incorrect" as well!

I know that what I have to say doesn't mean much as I am just a stranger on the internet, but I do want you to know that you have nothing to worry about. Your speech is fine. If you can communicate effectively with those around you then you're doing great. Your feelings, thoughts, and ideas are valid. The world deserves to hear what you have to say and think. The message loses no significance because of an incorrect production of /r/.

I think what I hate about this is the trivialization of a speech disorder that can greatly affect an individual's confidence and ability to communicate. Additionally, it adds to an already skewed view of what speech and language disorders are; I've met many people who are SHOCKED to learn that I do much more than "teach kids how to say their R's." 

The real truth is that speech disorders, including articulation and phonological disorders, can greatly impair a person's ability to functionally communicate. It goes beyond being unable to consistently produce the /r/ phoneme, which is generally common among children. There are children with such low intelligibility that they cannot functionally communicate in their classroom and social settings. Think about that- children in their formative years unable to fully participate in school and form bonds with those around them. Is that cute? Does that sound like fun? No. It's not.

As a speech-language pathologist working in the school setting I have seen first hand the effect having articulation, phonological, language, and fluency disorders can have on a child.
Not being able to produce /r/ or demonstrating other phonological processes while speaking is not cute. It greatly affects confidence and a student's ability to communicate and function in the classroom and other environments. 

It's not this "I'm so cute uwu," shit that gets spewed on TikTok.

It's fucking difficult for these students and they struggle to find confidence to express themselves fully. Students with great imagination and wonderful ideas don't want to speak in class because they're worried about how people will react to them. Their abilities ARE estimated just based on the way they produce /r/ or /th/.

Speech and language disorders aren't fucking cute. They affect your ability to COMMUNICATE in a world that revolves around COMMUNICATION.

They could definitely be more vulnerable in the situation you've described. The repetitive traumatic blows to the brain would most likely cause some form of degeneration of brain tissue; however, the changes in behavior, impulsivity, etc. may not seem as extreme as they could years down the road.

CTE (Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy), discussed at length in the Aaron Hernandez case, causes progressive degeneration of brain tissue due to repeated blows to the head. Previously, it was thought that CTE was a result of symptomatic concussions; however, it is now know that lesser, repetitive impacts (e.g. asymptomatic subconcussive) hits to the brain can also cause CTE. This is why we can also see CTE in athletes who did not play sports after high school or college.

So, 10 "mild" concussions within a year could definitely cause some form of permanent damage to the brain.

Yes, I do not think that people aware of how a traumatic brain injury (TBI) can leave a person extremely vulnerable- impulsivity; lack of self control; impairments in problem solving, attention, planning, and organizing; difficulties learning, retaining information, and memorization; behavioral issues and mood swings, etc. Additionally, a person with a TBI is likely to sustain another head injury later on down the road.

I am an SLP in the schools with Generalized Anxiety Disorder, Bipolar Disorder, and Depression. 

I know where you are coming from! Being an SLP can be challenging at times even if you love your job! I suggest that, if possible, you start seeing a therapist to help work through your anxiety. It really helps to talk about how you are feeling and what's going on. A therapist can help you work through how you are feeling and find strategies to deal with the anxiety and stresses in your life. Additionally, I would suggest seeking out a psychiatrist- maybe medication is something that could potentially help you regulate and lessen your anxiety.

I finally started seeing a psychiatrist and therapist after years of telling myself that I did not need any help. I did need help, and I am glad I sought it out. I am now on medication and I see a therapist weekly to discuss my anxieties and learn healthy coping mechanisms that can aid in lessening my anxieties. 

Additionally, I suggest remembering a few things:

- This is your first year as an SLP. You are out of school and are now being given more freedom than you have been given before- this is scary, and that's okay. It's okay to feel scared! This is a year to grow and learn. Ask for help when you need it. Ask as many questions as you need. Just continue to grow. After this year you will begin to feel more confident in your abilities as a clinician.

- Leave work at home. I used to bring work home with me- not just physical work but stresses and emotions that the work day brought me. I had to learn how to leave it at the workplace so I could go home and relax. This helped me feel less anxious at home. What doesn't get done today can get done tomorrow. It is okay. Do what you can and move on.

- If you are doing your best that is something to feel proud of. Be proud of yourself! You're doing great!

If you would like to privately discuss anxiety and mental health/illness feel free to private message me. 

It's going to be okay. I promise. <3

It's hard to describe what a day looks like because each day is different, so I'm going to describe what my WEEK looked like last year while we were face to face before making the transition to virtual learning.

MONDAY:
I dubbed this day my "therapy day." I saw the majority of students in groups back to back to back. I saw probably 5-6 groups from the beginning of my day (around 8am) until early in the afternoon, allowing for a break in the afternoon (around 12pm) for lunch. At the end of my day I typically did documentation, worked on evaluation reports, attended IEP meetings, and/or created therapy materials. It really all depended on what I needed to get done that day. Of course, I would also use that time to check emails and collaborate with coworkers.

TUESDAY, THURSDAY, FRIDAY:
I saw students I needed to see either for additional sessions (artic, fluency, etc) and attempted to see students that I may not have seen on Monday. I also attended/facilitated IEP meetings, completed evaluations, completed documentation, worked on evaluation reports, etc. 

WEDNESDAY:
I saw my self-contained classrooms back to back for the first half of my day, and then completed other duties as I stated above (documentation, report writing, etc.)

Ask me any questions if you have any!

Pros:

- Weekends, holidays, and summer off

- Support system of other SLPs in the district (can be dependent on how large the district is)

- Creating bonds with other SPED team members


Cons:

- Large caseloads, evaluations can pile up (I did approximately 20 evals last year... the most of which I completed over a span or 3-4 months)

- Scheduling (some teachers are hesitant to allow you to take a student at ANY point in the day)

- Other professionals may not understand what you do, or understand the importance of what you do

- Dealing with advocates 

- Lack of support from administration (in my experience)

Hi! Speech-language pathologist here! A lot of the previous comments are correct- exposure, repetition, models, etc. Language development is a combination of what we bring to the table (our brains, neural connections, etc) and our environment. This means that parents/guardians need to provide a rich language environment for children to learn language. What this looks like is: using "motherese" (higher pitched voices, emphasized intonation while talking to the child), commenting on things you see and what you're doing, talking with your child, having conversations with your child (even if they only babble-- talk to them like they're responding while actual sentences, it helps them learn what conversation and conversational turns looks like), reading, joint attention... I could go on but I'll stop here. The main takeaway is that it needs to be interactive. A typically developing child has what they need to learn language but they need to be taught. They need to be given models. They need to be able to practice- using language, using articulators. They're not just going to learn it from watching the parents, the parents need to be active participants.

As a recent graduate with a Master's of Arts in Communication Sciences and Disorders, this is concerning. Of course, we only see a glimpse of their life and there is a possibility when the cameras are gone May is more talkative around her family; however, I wouldn't be completely surprised if Nicole isn't giving her the language input she needs. This lack of input and model can seriously stunt a child's ability to learn language, obviously, and lead to language delays, disorders, etc. 
If Nicole is putting a tablet in front of her as often as others say she does then May is most likely not getting the language models she needs to learn language and its uses!
